whys.guess: TCP's unacked demand settles at the class-queue cap plus the 10-packet device queue (4+10=14, 100+10=110), so drops occur only while the cap sits below what Cubic's ACK clock tries to push in a burst; at q1000 the demand stays under the 1000-packet cap, which is how TCP holds 476 Mbps with zero drops and zero retransmissions.

whys.result: In every scheduler run udp_loss_frac equals 1 - udp_goodput/2e9 to six decimals (r010 0.755288, r012 0.746032, r013 0.755237) and mean tcp_bps+udp_bps is 965.9-971.8 Mbps, i.e. the link (T44, T45).

decisions.reason: Work-conserving scheduler: TCP takes ~476 Mbps, UDP takes the rest (sums 965.9-971.8 Mbps), and udp_loss_frac = 1 - udp_goodput/2e9 exactly (0.755288).
TCP's own ACK-clocked demand self-limits just below the class-queue cap (mean 949.92, max 952 of 1000), and the scheduler gives that class dedicated service, so no TCP packet is tail-dropped.
At q4 the class queue (cap 4, mean 1.92) is far below Cubic's ACK-clocked burst demand (inflight max 14 packets = cap + 10-packet device queue), so bursts overflow it 3416 times.
Work-conserving scheduler: q4 TCP payload is 12.6 Mbps lower and UDP takes exactly that (507935680 vs 489424320), with loss = 1 - share/2Gbps.

The 100-packet cap holds the TCP backlog (max 100 vs 952) so mean RTT falls to 2.09 ms from 17.22 ms; the recovered time lets the smaller inflight deliver 1.16% more, while the scheduler share keeps both near 480 Mbps.
H10 measures how long each class queue sits at its cap (q4 above 3.5, q100 above 95), which is what decides whether q100's 71 drops are rare bursts over a cap above the burst size.

answer.observations: E9/C10/V10 refuted H10; Y30 fits the q4/q100 drop pattern, and scheduler q100 TcpCubic remains the best measured TCP goodput at 482007923 bps.

decisions.reason: q100's 100-packet class queue absorbs Cubic's ACK-clocked bursts (inflight max 110 packets), while q4's 4-packet cap is below those bursts, causing many more TCP drops.
The q4 queue is full only in short bursts (1.2 s above 3.5 packets), but 1.2 s at TCP's rate is enough to drop thousands of packets; ACK-clocking keeps the mean queue low.

q100 keeps a steady TCP backlog above 3.5 packets for the whole interval but reaches the 100-packet cap only briefly (1.5 s), so drops are rare; this matches its 2.1 ms RTT and 110-packet inflight cap.

report.goal: Maximize tcp_goodput_bps, the brief's given goal.
report.limit: At scheduler q100 TcpCubic, TCP is limited by the scheduler's work-conserving per-flow share (about 480 Mbps of the 1 Gbps link) while UDP's 2 Gbps overload consumes the rest; queue length only trades TCP drops (q4) against backlog/RTT (q1000). Evidence E4, E5, E7, T44, T45, T57. q100 is best among tested scheduler queue lengths, not a proof that no untested length or TCP type is slightly better.
report.explanation: In the original FIFO, UDP offered 2 Gbps saturates l1, keeps the queue full, and tail-drops TCP, so all tested TCP types stay at or below 5792 bps. Replacing the sender FIFO with a scheduler gives each flow a service share, so Cubic reaches 476-482 Mbps while UDP takes the unused capacity. Queue length then matters only through TCP's class queue: q4 is below Cubic's ACK-clocked burst (inflight max 14 packets = 4 queue + 10 device queue) and drops 3416 TCP packets; q1000 permits a 952-packet backlog and 17.2 ms RTT; q100 caps the backlog at 100 packets (inflight max 110, RTT 2.1 ms) with only 71 drops, giving the highest measured goodput.

claims.text: In the original FIFO, UDP overload starves TCP: no tested TCP type exceeds 5792 bps.
A sender-side scheduler replacing the FIFO raises TCP goodput to hundreds of Mbps.
Under the scheduler, Cubic fills the scheduler share better than BBR, while UDP takes the unused capacity.
q100 is the best tested scheduler queue length: q4 loses to TCP drops, q1000 loses to backlog/RTT, and q100 is 1.16% above q1000.
The scheduler is work-conserving: TCP and UDP together use about the whole link, and TCP's rate is about its scheduler share.

The q4 drop count is compatible with only 1.2 s above 3.5 packets because drops occur in short full-queue bursts; q100's queue is usually above 3.5 but near the 100-packet cap only 1.5 s, giving 71 drops.
